rv.q: What a triumph Duncan-Brewster has, using her particular gift of conveying power without effort.
The alchemy that Duncan-Brewster and Squires have cooked up together in a week marks a fitting end to a uniquely unlucky, uniquely brilliant piece of theatre.
The play finds its footing by the second act and is well worth the wait, with some hair-raising set pieces.
Yet its dissection of Britain’s tangled relationship with race feels vital.

This passage is fantastic and, as in the previous works, what’s great is the frankness of the play’s portrayal of ordinary people trying to find their place in modern Britain and navigate a legacy that is none of their making.
This final instalment is the most flawed, but the Death of England project has proved a mighty, rapid-response record of an explosive period.
The first half is a rambling affair, with monologue and dialogue deployed as the two offer their takes on each other and their men.
The writing, though, isn’t quite as taut; over the course of more than two and a half hours, the evening drifts.

Clint Dyer (who also directs) and Roy Williams have constructed an electrifying and fulfilling final chapter with all the bitterness of tricky in-law (or in-sin, as described here) connections and also respect between two women who will barely admit it.
This is tremendous new writing about a business closing, but it’s also a story about hearts opening.

Closing Time has been unfortunate in that it has – like the entire sequence – been affected by Covid. Illness caused the postponement of its opening night and the cancellation of some performances. Jo Martin, the actress originally cast as Denise, has been replaced by Sharon Duncan-Brewster who takes to the stage script in hand.
They are productions of which the National Theatre can be justly proud.
These two performers are on sparkling form and give an edge and meaning to what comes across as a rather bitter polemic.
The play meanders just when it might more profitably go in for the kill, but both actresses seize their set-pieces with a vigour that is quite astonishing to behold.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this final chapter of Williams & Dyer's state-of-the-nation tetralogy as a worthy, emotionally resonant conclusion, with standout performances from Duncan-Brewster and Squires, though some find it overly didactic.
